content: Aluminium hydroxide, chemically represented as Al(OH)3, is the most stable form of aluminium under standard conditions. In nature, it occurs as the mineral gibbsite, also referred to as hydrargillite. Related compounds include aluminium oxide hydroxide (AlO(OH)) and aluminium oxide (Al2O3), which differ primarily by the loss of water molecules. Together, these compounds constitute the primary components of bauxite, the principal ore of aluminium. Structurally, gibbsite exhibits a typical metal hydroxide configuration, characterized by hydrogen bonding. It is composed of double layers of hydroxyl groups, with aluminium ions occupying two-thirds of the octahedral voids between these layers. Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric, meaning it can react with both acids and bases. When dissolved in acid, it forms Al(H2O)6³⁺ or its hydrolysis products. In strong alkaline solutions, it dissolves to form Al(OH)4⁻. Industrially, aluminium hydroxide is produced as an intermediate in the Bayer process, which is used for the extraction of aluminium metal. Pharmacologically, aluminium hydroxide is employed as an antacid under brand names such as Alu-Cap, Aludrox, or Pepsamar. It neutralizes excess gastric acid in the stomach, thereby reducing acidity. This reduction in stomach acidity can alleviate symptoms associated with ulcers, heartburn, or dyspepsia. However, its use may lead to constipation, which is why it is often combined with magnesium carbonate, a compound with laxative properties that counterbalance this effect. Additionally, aluminium hydroxide is used to manage elevated phosphate levels in the blood of patients with kidney failure. In immunology, aluminium hydroxide (commonly referred to as Alhydrogel) is utilized as an adjuvant in vaccines. It enhances the induction of a robust antibody (Th2) response. However, it has limited efficacy in stimulating cellular (Th1) immune responses, which are critical for protection against various pathogens. There is ongoing concern regarding the potential neurotoxicity of aluminium compounds. Aluminium has been detected in the brain lesions of individuals with Alzheimer’s disease, raising the possibility that excessive consumption of aluminium compounds may contribute to the development of Alzheimer’s or other neurodegenerative disorders. Elevated aluminium levels in the blood, such as those resulting from kidney dialysis using well water with high aluminium content, have been associated with a form of dementia that resembles but is likely distinct from Alzheimer’s disease. However, this hypothesis remains controversial and is the subject of ongoing scientific debate.
